newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: FEATURE - Used clothes make a mark in Central America.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Used clothes make a mark in Central America.

text.p: Until recently, even poor Central Americans felt too ashamed to wear someone else's discarded clothes.

Now, unable to resist $1 to $2 price tags on items such as dresses, Guatemalans, Salvadorans, Hondurans and Costa Ricans of all backgrounds paw through huge piles of clothing at thousands of used-clothes stores that have proliferated since the mid-1980s.

In Costa Rica the middle class is getting in on the used clothes act. Sergio Chacon, an office manager for a bank, told Reuters he could not afford the suits that are obligatory at his office, which cost a minimum of $150 each. So his mother suggested he shop at the "Ropa Americana" stores, as used-clothing businesses are known there, and now he is the best-dressed man in the office, sporting $3 suits.
More than 90 percent of the clothing comes in bales from brokers in the United States, inspiring the name of a chain of used-clothes stores in El Salvador -- USA-2.
"Ninety percent of Guatemalans are consuming these clothes because new clothes are so expensive. Only the high class doesn't buy it," importer Patricia Milian said.
Guatemala's imports of used clothes have increased seven-fold since 1988, from approximately 2.2 million pounds (1 million kilos) to 15.4 million pounds (7 million kilos).

In El Salvador, used clothes imports tripled between 1993 and 1996. "The demand for used clothing in Latin America and worldwide is tenfold what it was three years ago. I think it has a lot to do with lowering of tariffs and restrictions," Carl Jones, a used clothes exporter in California, said.
IS EVERYBODY HAPPY? NO!
Not everyone is happy about the "pacas" (Spanish for bales), as used-clothes stores are known in Guatemala.

"Imports of used clothes are a competition that harms our small garment industry. We have asked for higher duties on these imports," said Rafael Cruz, president of the Honduran Association of Small and Medium Clothesmaking Industries.
Business groups in Costa Rica, El Salvador and Guatemala echo the calls for higher import duties on used clothes.

"They are taking advantage of poverty. Maybe for the United States this is some type of recycling and they think they are doing people a favour, but they're just ruining the economy," said Donald Rodas, who makes T-shirts and underwear in his struggling home factory in Guatemala City.
Rodas said cheap used clothes have pushed him and other manufacturers to the verge of bankruptcy. Since 1991 he has gone from employing 60 people to 16.
The Guatemalan Chamber of Industry blames used clothes imports for the closing of 55 cloth mills in the country since 1990, doing away with 50,000 direct and indirect jobs.

Rodas leads an association of small manufacturers pushing for higher tariffs. The group has persuaded the government to form an economic commission to study the matter but government officials say they will not block imports.
"It is very difficult to justify prohibiting used clothes imports so the line of thought is to regulate, not prohibit," said Economy Minister Juan Mauricio Wurmser.
CLOSER INSPECTIONS URGED
He said regulation will not mean higher tarrifs but stiffer health standards as well as better control at customs and opening bales to ensure no new clothes are hidden inside.
Reni Bake, executive director of the textile guild of the Chamber of Industry, said her organisation supported that sort of regulation.

But Milian, manager of Trans Global Recycling, one of 12 big importers that bring in 70 percent of Guatemala's used clothes, is fighting any sort of restrictions. She said she cannot afford to rebale clothes if they are opened and the 30 percent import tax on used clothes is high enough already.

She said it costs $300 to import a bale of "guaranteed acceptable quality" clothes, which she sells for an average $600 to rural entrepreneurs who drive bales out to small towns to sell out of the back of their pickups on market day.
Milian and other importers in Central America buy from brokers such as Jones' Southern Textile company in California, who sells 100-pound (45-kilo) bales for an average of $.85 a pound (.5 kilo).
Jones, said he believed Latin American countries were best off adopting an open market strategy. "If they would lighten up and let these guys do business, the market will tell them what to do."
